This is an unpublished program submission for the $100 "Arcadian" program cash prize.  This program is from the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

The "Arcadian" submission letter and listing are available online, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#GraphicsQuadruplicate

Here is the program's brief description from the LISTing of the program:

This program uses right angle lines and XY operator to create unusual and very fast graphic art. The program was created to run in AB. It will run in BB, however the effect of speed of operation is lost. The redundancy of LINE statements is deliberate in order to increase the speed of operation.

4 colors are shown in parts 1 & 3 and 8 in part 2.

The following short message is on the program load screen:

Using right angle lines & XY operator to create unusual & very fast graphic art.  As many as 12 colors at once in parts 2 & 3.

The program begins with this message:

The order of the program is:

Graphics Quadruplicate

Order of program

(1) Mirror Images
(2) Quads at Odds
(3) Quadruplets Program Repeats

Enjoy!

C-8 - 16K All Line Art
Stanley Kendall
November 1983

This line art video is nearly two hours long!

Stan Kendall compiled many (perhaps all) of his random line art programs into one 16K program that runs under Blue Ram BASIC.  The first five videos in this series show the random art, while the sixth video shows the BASIC program listing in both the large font (which is the same as Bally BASIC's font) and smaller font (used in Blue Ram BASIC).

Remember, if you run this program then you will get different results.  I allowed each design to run several times before advancing to the next design in the series, but if there is one design that you like best, then there is no reason to advance.

The total video time for all six parts of "C-8 - 16K All Line Art" is 1 hr. 54 min.

You can view and/or download all of the parts of the video on archive.org here:

Part 1 (17:23) - (Designs 1-10 of 57):

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-1of6

Part 2 (18:22) -(Designs 11-20 of 57):

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-2of6

Part 3 (11:36) - (Designs 21-30 of 57):

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-3of6

Part 4 (19:51) - (Designs 31-40 of 57):

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-4of6

Part 5 (30:05) - (Designs 40-57 of 57):

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-5of6

Part 6 (17:18) - (BASIC Listing in Large and Small Font)

https://archive.org/details/C-816KAllLineArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtBRBBallyAstrocade1983-6of6

Here is the description from the beginning of the program when it is running before any of the 57 designs are displayed:

C-8  16K ALL LINE ART

TR(1) TO ADVANCE ALL DESIGNS

I HOPED TO PROG. ALL
THE BASIC LINE ART
POSSIBLE, BUT EVIDENTLY
THE LIMIT IS TOO HIGH.

SINCE THERE SOME 50+ DESIGNS IN THIS
PROGRAM YOU MAY WANT TO STOP AND
VIEW SOME RANDOM WITH A GOSUB
FROM THE KEYPAD.  THE DESIGNS START
@100 AND ARE EVERY 100 LINE NOS.

HOPE YOU ENJOYED THE ART

IT TAKES ALOT OF TIME TO WATCH

AND ONE REALLY NEVER SEES ALL
THE PATTERNS

THE ART IS LIMITED ONLY BY ONE'S

IMAGINATION!!!

16582:
Bally Christmas "Card"
By Ed Grobe (Edge Software)
Arcadian 5, no. 2 (Dec. 3, 1982): 29 AstroBASIC

This is unedited video art for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade and "AstroBASIC."  This is NOT a video overview.

https://archive.org/details/BallyChristmasCardEdGrobeUneditedVideoArtBallyAstrocade1982

This program draws a four-color Christmas tree on the screen, which is a neat trick for AstroBASIC, which can normally only display two colors (background and foreground).  The tree is draw slowly from top to bottom and left to right.  After the tree is completely displayed, then the lights flash and Christmas message appears.

Enjoy!

Adam
16583:
The Tin Pants Gang
By Mike White
Niagara Bugs Club Tape 1. March 1985.
December 1982 (Original Bally BASIC version)

This is unedited video art (it's actually a simple three-minute cartoon) for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade and "AstroBASIC."  This is NOT a video overview.

https://archive.org/details/TheTinPantsGangMikeWhiteUneditedVideoArtAstroBASICBallyAstrocade1985

This is a simple animated cartoon written in BASIC.  Since the program draws the animated completely in BASIC without using any machine language routines, the graphics "blink."  This is normal and would look this way on a CRT television.

The following title is displayed as the program loads:

The Tin Pants Gang
Produced and Directed
by Mike White
and Starring:
Rusty Raygun
and his friends:
Colonel Oosescrews
Rd D2 - Oilly Slick
June Kyard
Thirsty Enfile
and the Martians!!

Program Instructions:

There are 3 clues to aid you in understanding what's happening:
  1. Remember, this is a cartoon, it's supposed to be silly
  2. Turn the sound up a bit.  Don't miss anything
  3. The robots appear in the same order as their names
     (on the title screen) [The marquee]
(Press any key to see a "rerun")

Enjoy!

Adam
16584:
M-III - "Box Art"
By Stanley Kendall.
Arcadian 5, no. 3 (Jan. 14, 1983): 45.

This is unedited video art for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade and "AstroBASIC."  This is NOT a video overview.

https://archive.org/details/M-IIIBoxArtStanleyKendallUneditedVideoArtAstroBASICBallyAstrocade1983

This random video art program was written February 23, 1982. Unlike many video art programs, this one ends after about four minutes and twenty seconds.  The program is only called "M-III," but to give it a better description, it has been dubbed "M-III - 'Box Art.'"

Paul Thacker notes: "The [M-III] program is a fairly simple graphical demo. It draws different size boxes vertically and horizontally, and makes some interesting patterns."

Enjoy!

Adam

16587:
More Line Art.
By Stanley Kendall.
January, 1985.

This is unedited video art for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade and Blue Ram BASIC.  This is NOT a video overview.

https://archive.org/details/MoreLineArtStanleyKendallVideoArtBallyAstrocade1985

I've attached a screenshot of the art while it's in the process of drawing.  I should have been attaching screenshots like this all along with these posts.

More Line Art draws one vertical line at a time horizontally across the screen.  The background color is light blue (Blue Ram BASIC's default color) and the foreground colors are green, blue and red.  As this program draws from left to right, triangles begin to appear, slowly growing smaller.  It's a neat, if slow, effect.

This 13-line video art program has no random elements.  In this example, the program runs for about ten minutes.  If the program is run longer, it seems that the triangles continue to grow smaller and then will, I think, begun to grow larger again.

16594:
Graphic Pictures
By Video Wizards (Ken Springsteen)
March 1982

These are video graphics/computer art for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade for use with "AstroBASIC," the version of Bally BASIC with the built-in tape interface.

This video overview shows 11 programs loading and displaying detailed mono-colored pictures on the TV screen.  The video begins with an overview, background and brief history of Video Wizards.

Here it is on YouTube:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cVf9yhjU3eM

Here is a link to the video on Archive.org (where you can view it and/or download it):

https://archive.org/details/GraphicPicturesVideoWizardsOverviewBallyAstrocadeAstroBASIC1982

Note that no program called "Graphic Pictures" was released on tape.  Rather, Ken Springsteen, the programmer, had an unusual method of distributing his software along with the six programs that he wrote:

1) Jekyl & Hyde
2) Multi-Graphics
3) Crypt-O-Grams
4) The Exterminator
5) Slow Machine
6) Lazer Brains

These eleven pictures have been gathered into one video for easy reference and viewing.  The graphic programs do allow the graphics to be changed by the user with, as Paul Thacker (who archived these programs) describes it, "a rather cumbersome interface."  The method to change the graphics is not shown here, nor are any BASIC program listings for the programs.

The video is broken down into several sections:

0:00 - Overview of Video Wizards and Graphic Pictures

The following are the eleven pictures in this video

7:19 - Welcome to the World of Video Wizards
7:53 - Thank You for Ordering Software from Video Wizards
8:16 - Charlie (The Man of 1,000 Faces)
8:39 - Arcadian Logo
9:05 - Hot Rod Customizing Center
9:34 - Space Creatures
10:01 - Susie (The Girl of 1,000 Faces)
10:24 - Home Sweet Home
10:48 - Puppy-Vision
11:12 - Professional Arcade Graphic
11:40 - Go-Go Dancer

12:04 - End Credits

The video has a 1/2 page newspaper advertisement for the Astrocade with the Z-GRASS unit.  This is from the Winnipeg Free Press's October 9, 1982 issue.  There are three other ads from the Arcadian.

Ken Springsteen, the man who programmed these graphics, left the Astrocade scene by around June 1982, when he put up his collection for sale.  This means his "company," Video Wizards, was only in business for three to four months.

Enjoy!

Adam

Increasingly, people want content and connections coming directly to them, and this is why we continue to invest in Yahoo Mail -- including the recent launch of a new Yahoo Mail app<http://service.comms.yahoo.net/T/v40000016e160b4fabb43f886e96c65220/517b2cc4badc49720000021ef3a0bcc2/517b2cc4-badc-4972-a001-b0c7099edcd6?__dU__=v0G4RBKTXg2GvzBXXO0iqzhQD4bfSOAnZx&__F__=v0fUYvjHMDjRPMSh3tviDHXIoXcPxvDgUUCCPvXMWoX_1c5OGBAFPGWRLtePbym4Jo-rHoYmNTevg8rH_BooC1L07AGPcn7d9FlQ7nNymjFepTgUJp7zeFo-QZ_6QGTD3wwpd0EiCPongWA8HE3fu4BF7R7b90sPQpPoVHFAMpSUjGKq-RMonZayBCGhP7eH3YJBY8FIVeJlq7MNbF22miJ-KUKgFROBpaOSEJRMY51o_ISQtTm6pPp-URpufuB6-KD9O0Uu8Mt0Zro5FH0_Kn05oL9S8DS3sN> that is currently the highest-rated email app in the App Store and Google Play.

So, as our users’ habits have evolved, we have begun the process of evolving our approach to help active Yahoo Groups thrive and migrate to our email platform. To help you plan for these changes, below is the schedule of how this transition will happen.

Beginning October 28, 2019:

  *   Users will be able to join a Yahoo Group only through an invite from the Group Moderator or by submitting a request to join a Group, which requires approval by the Group Moderator.
  *   Since we are moving Group communication from posting on message boards to email distribution, uploading and hosting of new content will also be disabled on the Yahoo Groups website.

Beginning December 14, 2019:

  *   All Groups will be made private and any content that was previously uploaded via the website will be removed. We believe privacy is critical and made this decision to better align with our overall principles.
  *   If you would like to keep any of the content you’ve posted or stored in the past within your Yahoo Group, please download it by December 14 by accessing this link<http://service.comms.yahoo.net/T/v40000016e160b4fabb43f886e96c65220/517b2cc4badc49720000021ef3a0bcc3/517b2cc4-badc-4972-a001-b0c7099edcd6?__dU__=v0G4RBKTXg2GvzBXXO0iqzhQD4bfSOAnZx&__F__=v0fUYvjHMDjRPMSh3tviDHXIoXcPxvDgUUCCPvXMWoX_0DA16EdUMykOxW2gVCnxDU5cHx-QK3QTtoTSEFskCd7V1LSW30ORTEac7C7l1fJ1QloWG7xy2htV8dLg14Xm6qCnbebc5k5F2H2ylwiJ2VZhtSqPP35IvMc55oxGKhFK4uBS5LWWYTo4oIHpxnyUih9JCs_zKLp6GVBMLRCAGKlSObr3xc7dUQVH6Io0XoMus8whCpPOrU85sonosok7emXNjM3xEMUnFt2guByNaDDCXEkoIP-WUvv_IU-CHUlng=>.

As these dates get closer, we will send follow-up reminders. More information about the upcoming changes can be found here<http://service.comms.yahoo.net/T/v40000016e160b4fabb43f886e96c65220/517b2cc4badc49720000021ef3a0bcc4/517b2cc4-badc-4972-a001-b0c7099edcd6?__dU__=v0G4RBKTXg2GvzBXXO0iqzhQD4bfSOAnZx&__F__=v0fUYvjHMDjRPMSh3tviDHXIoXcPxvDgUUCCPvXMWoX_30tcPSLyBQEa0klOzPQdng8h8pYsOOPIzEGVMPtE8Jl_ezvcJ3kY1QZleSAk4Bb5JpzsLuXV8nVCWhYbvHLaG1Xx0uDXhebqoKdt5tzmTkXYfbKXCInZVmG1Ko8_fki8xznmjEYqEUri4FLktZZhOjiggenGfJSKH0kKz_MounoZUEwtEIAYqVI5uvfFzt1RBUfoijRegy6zzCEKk86tTz-bHKIKNo4fwkVUMPr2SCjH_5VrUXmS-6bZqFadGNYHW_8hT4IdSWeA==>.

While this evolution of Yahoo Groups is inspired by how we see the platform being used today, we know change can be difficult. Here are a few important facts as we make this transition:

1. Yahoo Groups is not going away - We know that our users are deeply passionate about connecting around shared interests, and we are evolving Groups to better align with how you use it today.

2. New groups can still be formed - Users can continue to connect with others around their common bonds and interests. From animal rescues to sporting and activity groups, civic organizations to local PTAs, members of our Yahoo Groups will remain connected and able to share their activities and interests. All of the content that you have shared previously on the website, can continue to be shared via email.

We know that Yahoo Groups is an important online extension of your real-life group of friends, interests and communities, and we are committed to supporting communities that rely on Yahoo Groups. Thanks for coming along with us this far. We look forward to seeing where the technology -- and you -- take us in the decades to come.

Thanks to a generous donation, there will be another episode of the Astrocast coming in the next few weeks.

With the donation, there was a note that said:

"Whatever is left-over, feel free to use it to pay future fees, support your website, restart your podcast, or whatever you deem appropriate -- podcast preferred, but that's just me... ;-)"

I'm not naming the person who made the donation, but if this persons wants to have their name made public, then please step forward here and say hellow.

If, given that Adam (me!) has wanted to make another episode of the Astrocast, a person steps up, donates money and then says, "Hey, man, make another episode of the Astrocade.  It's just a suggestion, but I'll break your legs if one doesn't come out soon."  Okay, no one said that exactly, but just the hint that people want to hear my sad little voice again is enough to inspire me.

The next episode of the podcast isn't going to cover a game or Astrocade history.  Given the circumstances, I'm going to cover the Astrocade community and how, no matter its small size, it's still here after all these years.  I may ask for the community's help with feedback about why people stick by the Astrocade despite its weirdness and flaws.  More on this later-- hopefully next week.

Adam

16635:
Michael Matte updated me again on November 28, 2019.

Here are Michael's comments (followed by comments from me):

----------------------------------------

I have run some tests on my hi-res multi-pager. For example, while viewing page 0, which displayed narrow hi-res vertical colored stripes on the screen, a second program was written to page 1 and then viewed after a 5 second time delay. This second program was used during the development of my hi-res static RAM scheme. The program utilizes variations of the magic functions and "writes" 15 graphic patterns on the screen. A large fish aquarium is also written. I found out that anytime you are utilizing the magic xor/or functions to write graphic patterns to a specific page, the multi-pager output port 75H must be pointing to that page for writes and also reads. Otherwise, the magic hardware will not be able to read that page for the xor/or logical operations. So far, the multi-pager is working as expected.

I am now working on an 8 page test/demonstration demo. I'm not sure how many 1K bytes this demo will require. This demo will be in the 2000H cartridge form allowing up to 8KB to be used. Page 0 will display first the demo text intro. While viewing this page, the other 7 pages will be written to with static graphics. There will also be a short "move critter" program copied to the page 7 scratchpad area. After the page 0 text intro view time counts down to zero (or any key on the keypad is pressed), the multi-pager will start flipping through each page nonstop. View time will start at about 10 seconds. After a pass of viewing all 8 pages, the view time for each pass of 8 pages will decrease. The multi-pager will just keep flipping thru each page faster and faster, down to 1 second (or less?) per page. I am hoping to add an audio "flip" sound to each page flip to make the demo more entertaining.

When this page view time counts down to its minimal view time, page flipping will cease. Then the "move critter" program in page 7 will be executed. The critter will be seen moving through each of the 8 pages of graphics "erasing" the graphics as the critter moves.

Once the critter finishes erasing graphics in page 7, a hi-res fish demo similar to the low-res fish demo in BalcheckHR will run on page 7. Depending on how many of the 8K bytes are available for this fish demo, I am hoping to use up the remaining bytes to move around the screen multiple varieties/sizes of fish. This fish demo will perhaps test the limitations of moving multiple large patterns, say 16 pixels wide by 18 pixel lines high (or larger?), around the screen using the normal  Z80 data block transfer LDIR instruction (opcode ED B0).

The fish demo will run for 2:00 minutes, then a jump back to the multi-pager demo will be executed to repeat the demos again. A viewer will have the option to run the fish demo nonstop by pressing any key on the keypad, in which case, an elapsed timer 00:00:00 will appear at the bottom of the screen. Pushing the system reset button will also start up the multi-pager demo.

Below is a listing of the hi-res static graphics that will appear on each of the 8 pages during the execution of the multi-pager demo.

Page Page Graphics

  0 Demo Text Intro
  1 Narrow Vertical Stripes
  2 Aquarium +15 Magic Writes
  3 "Multiple Page Demo" Title Page
  4 Narrow Horizontal Stripes
  5 Textured 10 Color Test Pattern
  6 Narrow Vertical + Horizontal Stripes
  7 Hi-Res Gunfight Snapshot

Based on what I've seen the multi-pager do so far, the above program description is feasible. I look forward to seeing just how fast the multi-pager can flip thru pages without any problems. I think this 8KB hi-res demo package is going to be really cool to watch.

Bye.
MCM

----------------------------------------

16641:
I added the modified version of "Gobblers" for "AstroBASIC" to BallyAlley.com.  This program was originally written by Bob Wiseman in 1981. Klaus Doerge modified this version of the game in 1983.

This 2-player game requires you to eat a bunch of squares, where each square has one to four points in it, resulting in a score of 1 to 4 for each one eaten. They are positioned in a 5 x 10 grid, and you utilize the JX and JY directions of your controller to move your man. Of course, your opponent is doing the same. The computer is keeping score. It is listed in Bally BASIC, but plays in 'AstroBASIC' as well, just a bit faster."

You can download it here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#GobblersBobWisemanAB

This is the modified version of the program, which I converted from the 300-baud, Bally BASIC version.  This WAV file has been cleaned with BallyBin/AstroWAV 1.4.  It loads using "AstroBASIC" either on real hardware or emulation.

Enjoy!

Adam

Wait for an official announcement from Yahoo before slacking off your downloading!

Whither PGO when Verizon finally pulls the plug?

Plans are afoot to transition PGO to a new data source and a new revenue model.

PGO's Achilles heel has always been its perpetual licence.

Perpetual licences are OK for Paint programs but not for an app that depends on a 3rd party data source that could change at any time.

Therefore, moving forward, the new PGO will transition to multiple data sources starting with Groups.io and Facebook groups (maybe also Google groups & phpBB) and it will move to a subscription model.

If you didn't register in the last 12 months but do have PGO then to move to the new PGO will be $10.

You can stay with the old PGO.  It'll still read, sort & search your existing downloaded YG data.

And you can swap data with other PGO users using the Export & Import functions.

Moving to the new PGO is not mandatory.

Cheers,

Wilson.

For any enthusiasts who are going to Magfest or live on the east coast, Rachel Simone Weil and I will be running a history panel all about the independent developer/enthusiast scene that cropped around the Astrocade! Obviously quite unique for a game console to have vastly more unofficial, "bedroom coder" style software releases than official ones, and having enthusiast-developed and sold hardware is similarly incredible. We'll be talking about how this scene coalesced, the kind of unique, even artful programs that were created, how it petered out, and if there's time, even a bit about the current state of homebrew development for the platform.
I also plan on bringing my Astrocade to the museum area and having it set up to play immediately following the panel with some BASIC games and homebrew/indie stuff on the ultimulti. Magfest is Jan. 2-5 in National Harbor, Maryland, and the panel itself will be recorded and posted on YouTube in the weeks following the event.

16650:
It's funny that we're talking about Blue Ram BASIC programs, because this morning I loaded the 300-baud version of "Gobblers (Mod)" into Blue Ram BASIC to see if it would run faster.  This can be done if you have the following hardware/software: an Astrocade, a Blue Ram expansion, the Blue Ram BASIC 1.1 cartridge (or a multicart), and the 300-baud interface.  There aren't many people with all of that stuff, but if you do have it, then the process works fine.

To load the 300-baud program into BRB, I typed the following command:

:INPUT 300

As expected, the program loaded fine.  It's neat to see a 300-baud program load with the small font.

I was hoping that the modified version of "Gobblers" might work without changes-- but it just looks weird.  I guess this has something to do with background/foreground-only "colors" of Bally BASIC having issues with the four available colors in BRB (Ken, I expect you know what I'm talking about-- can you offer a better explanation?).  The game seems to play properly (overlooking the strange colors and non-erasing of background objects), but I'm not sure if it runs faster.  Without putting forth some effort into making changes to the program, this is a game that I'll not see running properly in BRB.

Adam

This obviously isn't the first time that I've tried to shine a spotlight onto "The Pits" to give it some well-deserved attention.  In Episode 4 (August 2016) of the Bally Alley Astrocast, I covered this game with Chris (the podcast's co-host).  You can listen to that podcast here:

ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com
The object of "The Pits" is to move the small dot in the upper-left corner past the pits to the center of the medium-size box in the lower-right corner.  The clunker is that the pits move up the screen all the time and can catch you.  Each time the screen rolls up it counts as one move.  A successful trip in 16 moves is doing well.  This BASIC game is available for Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC" and can be downloaded from BallyAlley.com.

"The Pits" is a perfect example that gameplay is the true measure of a game's value and that graphics can be completely secondary to the core gameplay experience.

Adam

The Tin Pants Gang

and Starring:
Rusty Raygun
and his friends:
Colonel Oosescrews
Rd D2 - Oilly Slick
June Kyard
Thirsty Enfile
and the Martians!!

Program Instructions:

There are 3 clues to aid you in understanding what's happening:
  1. Remember, this is a cartoon, it's supposed to be silly
  2. Turn the sound up a bit.  Don't miss anything
  3. The robots appear in the same order as their names
     (on the title screen) [The marquee]
(Press any key to see a "rerun")

The program starts with two choices:

   #1 Twinkle X
   #2 Boxes

If you choose option 1, then you must give two input options: "Step Size" and "Box Size." Both of these options affect how the art looks.  Menu option two, "Boxes," doesn't ask for any options from the user.

Some brief notes from the 1984 publication of this program in the BUG newsletter:

"Notes - Stars twinkle best when B=2 TO 8 & E=6 TO 12
May other interesting variations possible.

"7/30/83 Slight modification.  Improved list of art and screen title.
This will create an attractive uncluttered screen.
The nice thing about ART of this type, and actually all ASTRO programs, is that it can always be changed, upgraded, improved, etc.  It also gives one new ideas."Niagara BUG Bulletin, 2, no. 1 (Jan. 1984): 4.

LeRoy Flamm wrote a BASIC program called "Plotter Drive Program" in 1985 that used a Penman plotter to draw a detailed space shuttle and a "robot" (really, it's R2-D2).  The plotter was connected to the Bally Arcade via an RS-232C serial input connected via the old Bally tape interface with a printer jack connection.

Here is a video of the Penman plotter in action (it's not connected to a Bally).

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mR8enP09RPI

Penman the plot robot<https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mR8enP09RPI>
Pen man has been build 1984. It's a portable plotter. http://www.tnotes.de/penman
www.youtube.com
Watching the Penman draw is almost a work of art, isn't it? The Penman plotter doesn't look anything like I suspected it would look.  I thought it would be big and clunky, like the plotter that was available in my high school drafting class in the 1980s.

Here is a review of the Penman plotter from "Electronic Systems News" (Autumn 1985): 19-20.:

C-8 - 16K All Line Art
Stanley Kendall
November 1983

This line art video is nearly two hours long!

Stan Kendall compiled many (perhaps all) of his random line art programs into one 16K program that runs under Blue Ram BASIC.  The first five videos in this series show the random art, while the sixth video shows the BASIC program listing in both the large font (which is the same as Bally BASIC's font) and smaller font (used in Blue Ram BASIC).

Remember, if you run this program then you will get different results.  I allowed each design to run several times before advancing to the next design in the series, but if there is one design that you like best, then there is no reason to advance.

The total video time for all six parts of "C-8 - 16K All Line Art" is 1 hr. 54 min.

16722:
So to follow up on this, the talk Rachel and I gave Friday went well, and folks seemed to really enjoy learning about an aspect of game history that few of them were familiar with!
We went over the technical aspects of the Astrocade, Bally and Astrovision's plans for the system with the add-under, the development of the BASIC cart and its usage as a way for enthusiasts to access the system, how it was reverse engineered and information got shared through enthusiast groups and newsletters, independently developed hardware expansions such as Blue RAM, Viper One, the Machine Language Manager cart, the ICBM controller, and how things finally started petering out in the mid-80s. Rachel also talked about the current state of Astrocade development tools and emulation and encouraged people to look into this unique and interesting machine, with its surprising power and musical ability for a 1977 platform.
We also showed clips of several programs, including the Diamond video art demo, Halloween Ghost, the Self Portrait art program, Goldfish Demo, The Tin Pants Gang, the Rockin Robin music program, Gravity, and some games - Artillery Duel, Treasure Cove, Cavern Quest, Candyman, Nuke the @^%^$!, and a couple others. Afterwards I had a few folks come over to the Magfest museum space, where I pulled out my Astrocade and BASIC/Ultimulti carts to run a few indie/homebrew games. Those in attendance in particular liked Candyman and War!
My thanks go out to ballyalley.com for being such a great resource for this panel, and to the folks I've been able to reach out to and talk with before the event to learn from their experiences. Hopefully I can interview more folks who were involved in the scene in the coming months! I added a program with an unknown name, dubbed "Colorful Circles."  The program is probably from about 1983 or so and was possibly written by Ed Horger.

"Colorful Circles" is video graphics/computer art for the Bally Arcade / Astrocade for use with VIPERsoft or Blue RAM BASIC.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V3AULOjeSCI

This unlabeled art program was found on Ed Horger's tape.  Paul Thacker dubbed the program "Colorful Circles."  This program runs for about 18 seconds before crashing.  Since the artistic display that is created during that brief 18 seconds of life is worth preserving, the program is included here.

This program ends with a syntax error (a "WHAT?") at line 11313.  The program attempts to print the line but it prints strange garage with many question marks.  The program is very short and ends with line 40 (I'm not sure why "line" 11313 is listed in the error message).  Perhaps this program is a work in progress.  Examine the BASIC program listing after the program runs to see what the issue might be that causes the error.

The technical side of the astrocade is the easiest background about the astrocade that can be conveyed to someone in an easy-to-understand manner. That's what most people count on hearing and it does a good job of getting the point across, somewhat, about the potential abilities of the system.

>>
[We also covered the] Bally and Astrovision's plans for the system with the add-under
>>

Once you begin to delve into the add-under, then the astrocade waters become very murky.  I wonder how you chose to deal with this computer upgrade in the talk.  There is so much information available about the add-under, the least of which includes the many different names and periods of time in which it might have been released during the Bally Arcade/Astrocade's lifetime.

>>
the development of the BASIC cart and its usage as a way for enthusiasts to access the system
>>

I hope that someday there is a documentary that covers the various Tiny BASIC versions that were released for various computers.  That BASIC variant allowed computers with only a small amount of RAM to have a language that beginning computer users could comprehend and use with minimal effort.  I'd still like to see Tiny BASIC ported to the Atari home computers.  There is a link about this idea in the Atari age forums, here:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/238779-tiny-basic-on-atari-8-bit/

>>
how it was reverse engineered and information got shared through enthusiast groups and newsletters
>>

One of the benefits that the Astrocade community enjoyed was that they had direct access, early on, about to how the onboard 8K ROM functioned.  This allowed them to use the subroutines in their own programs.  Also, schematics for the Bally Arcade were available (this was not unheard of at the time for most of the systems released during that era).

I don't think that JS&A get enough credit for the blossoming of the Bally Arcade community.  It's true that JS&A abandoned the astrocade early on, but their advertising seems to whet potential users appetites for a true computer, not just a game system.  The early Bally Arcade adopters, in order to reach the full potential of the "Arcade" had to have a do-it-yourself attitude.  And do-it-yourself they did as they created both hardware and software that never would have been released by the parent company (either Bally or Astrovision, Inc).

independently developed hardware expansions such as Blue RAM, Viper One

The three main RAM upgrades for the astrocade, when used in conjunction with one of the extended BASIC languages, really does give the Astrocade a computer-like feel.

the Machine Language Manager cart
>>

the ICBM controller
>>

Chris and I play ICBM Attack and review it on the to-be-released-soon Astrocade episode #12. how things finally started petering out in the mid-80s.

I don't even understand the exact ending of Astrocade, Inc., as the that story is muddled.  There is plenty of information out there on the Bally alley website, but I've never been able to wrap my head around how it all came to an end.

We went over the technical aspects of the Astrocade, Bally and Astrovision's plans for the system with the add-under, the development of the BASIC cart and its usage as a way for enthusiasts to access the system, how it was reverse engineered and information got shared through enthusiast groups and newsletters, independently developed hardware expansions such as Blue RAM, Viper One, the Machine Language Manager cart, the ICBM controller, and how things finally started petering out in the mid-80s. Rachel also talked about the current state of Astrocade development tools and emulation and encouraged people to look into this unique and interesting machine, with its surprising power and musical ability for a 1977 platform.

We also showed clips of several programs, including the Diamond video art demo, Halloween Ghost, the Self Portrait art program, Goldfish Demo, The Tin Pants Gang, the Rockin Robin music program, Gravity, and some games - Artillery Duel, Treasure Cove, Cavern Quest, Candyman, Nuke the @^%^$!, and a couple others. Those in attendance in particular liked Candyman and War!

My thanks go out to ballyalley.com for being such a great resource for this panel, and to the folks I've been able to reach out to and talk with before the event to learn from their experiences. Hopefully I can interview more folks who were involved in the scene in the coming months!

The following additional information is from the "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ"

The "ICBM Attack" cartridge was released into the public domain in 2001 by Brett Bilbrey, Mike Toth and Marian Nalepa (Spectre Systems).  The game requires a special hand controller to play - it cannot be played without it. In 1985, Marian Nalepa said that only about 125 of these cartridges were released because of the difficulty of hand-assembling the controller.

Paul Thacker was given access to recordings from BASIC cassettes in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection (the programmer of the game).  "I found that some of the recordings labeled ICBM Attack would process, but wouldn't load correctly into AstroBASIC using :INPUT. But then I tried loading them with :RUN, and voila, up pops ICBM Attack. Actually, it's more a demo of ICBM Attack." A ship flies around the screen, and you control a cursor using the special controller. You can fire from various ground defenses.  This creates an explosion at the spot of the cursor, but as far as I can tell you can't destroy the ship. Sometimes there will be an extra, unmovable cursor or two. Obviously it's a bit glitchy. I found two different versions. In one, the ship moves pretty slowly. In the other, the ship moves extremely fast." (Paul Tacker, Astrocade Discussion Group, Message #3024).  Paul adds "Also, after I posted that, I found an even earlier demo for Bally BASIC."  Designed by Brett Bilbrey.  Sound by Marion Nelepa.

This video can also be viewed or downloaded from Archive.org:

The following additional information is from the "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ"

The "ICBM Attack" cartridge was released into the public domain in 2001 by Brett Bilbrey, Mike Toth and Marian Nalepa (Spectre Systems).  The game requires a special hand controller to play - it cannot be played without it. In 1985, Marian Nalepa said that only about 125 of these cartridges were released because of the difficulty of hand-assembling the controller.

Paul Thacker was given access to recordings from BASIC cassettes in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection (the programmer of the game).  "I found that some of the recordings labeled ICBM Attack would process, but wouldn't load correctly into AstroBASIC using :INPUT. But then I tried loading them with :RUN, and voila, up pops ICBM Attack. Actually, it's more a demo of ICBM Attack." A ship flies around the screen, and you control a cursor using the special controller. The following additional information is from the "Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ"

The "ICBM Attack" cartridge was released into the public domain in 2001 by Brett Bilbrey, Mike Toth and Marian Nalepa (Spectre Systems).  The game requires a special hand controller to play - it cannot be played without it. In 1985, Marian Nalepa said that only about 125 of these cartridges were released because of the difficulty of hand-assembling the controller.

Paul Thacker was given access to recordings from BASIC cassettes in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection (the programmer of the game).  "I found that some of the recordings labeled ICBM Attack would process, but wouldn't load correctly into AstroBASIC using :INPUT. But then I tried loading them with :RUN, and voila, up pops ICBM Attack. Actually, it's more a demo of ICBM Attack." A ship flies around the screen, and you control a cursor using the special controller. You can fire from various ground defenses.  This creates an explosion at the spot of the cursor, but as far as I can tell you can't destroy the ship. Sometimes there will be an extra, unmovable cursor or two. Obviously it's a bit glitchy. I found two different versions. In one, the ship moves pretty slowly. In the other, the ship moves extremely fast." (Paul Tacker, Astrocade Discussion Group, Message #3024).  Paul adds "Also, after I posted that, I found an even earlier demo for Bally BASIC."  Designed by Brett Bilbrey.  Sound by Marion Nelepa.

Here is a direct link to ballyalley.com for the seventh article "In-Depth Look At... series" that concentrates on Custom Expand Patterns:

An In-Depth Look At... series: A Supplement to the "Nutting Manual"
for the Bally/Astrocade Computer
Part 7: Custom Expand Pattern.
By MCM Design (Michael Matte).
January 2020.

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/An_In-Depth_Look_At/An_In-Depth_Look_At.html#AnInDepthLookAtCustomExpandPattern

This lesson introduces the magic expand function, which allows a two color graphic pattern to be stored in one half the normal memory. For example, the Gunfight's graphic tree pattern seen on the TV screen is 2 bytes wide by 17 bytes high requiring a total of 34 bytes to be written (displayed) on the screen. This 2 color pattern, when utilizing the magic expand function, can be stored in memory using only 17 bytes, where in this case, each byte defines one horizontal pattern line of 2 bytes.

Here is a description of the included program example 7-1:

This example will write with expand one line of 2 bytes from just a single pattern byte. A single shifter byte will also be written at the end of this 2 byte expanded write so that the magic shifter can also be experimented with. The write with expand will occur 2 lines below a green reference byte located at the screen address 4014H, just like the magic writes in the previous lesson example programs. The reference byte will be written near the middle of the screen RAM area on the very first (top) line. The single pattern byte to be expanded, will be stored just below the program which begins at 4E10H.

I've also posted a link in the AtariAge forums:

https://atariage.com/forums/topic/293889-an-in-depth-look-at-series-nutting-manual-supplement/?do=findComment&comment=4444592

Enjoy!

Adam
